title: If our public-facing AI system started producing harmful output, how fast could we disable it?
description: A board-level oversight question testing whether an organization's incident-response capability for a publicly-facing AI system has actually been tested, not just planned.

history.note: Normalized US/UK spelling variants to the American-English house style (schema field names, e.g. organizations_involved, are already American; majority framework citations - NIST, FTC, EEOC, FCRA, BIPA - are American sources).

question_text: If our public-facing AI system began producing harmful or offensive output — through adversarial manipulation or otherwise — how quickly could we detect and disable it, and has that response actually been drilled, the way it was not before Microsoft's Tay chatbot was manipulated within hours of launch?
rationale: Tay went from launch to public, high-profile failure in under a day because there was no adversarial testing beforehand and no rehearsed rapid-disable capability once the manipulation was underway.
follow_up_actions: Request the most recent red-team test report and confirm it includes a timed kill-switch drill.
Confirm red-teaming specifically includes coordinated-manipulation scenarios, not just individual bad prompts.
Ask who has authority to trigger the kill switch and how quickly they can be reached.
